questions.question: What is erasure coding?

options.text: A secure data deletion method for compliance
A data protection method that breaks data into fragments, encodes with redundant pieces, enabling recovery from failures
A data compression algorithm for reducing storage costs
An encryption method for data at rest

questions.explanation: Erasure coding: split data into k fragments, generate m parity fragments. Any k of (k+m) fragments can reconstruct original. More storage-efficient than replication for same fault tolerance.

questions.question: How does erasure coding compare to replication for fault tolerance?

options.text: Erasure coding provides similar fault tolerance with less storage overhead

questions.explanation: 3x replication: 200% overhead, survives 2 failures. RS(10,4) erasure coding: 40% overhead, survives 4 failures. Erasure coding: better storage efficiency, but higher CPU for encode/decode.

questions.question: What is Reed-Solomon coding?

options.text: A data compression algorithm for storage efficiency
A widely-used erasure coding algorithm that can recover from multiple simultaneous failures
A lossless compression method for media files
A network protocol for reliable data transfer

questions.explanation: Reed-Solomon: most common erasure code. RS(k,m): k data chunks, m parity chunks. Survives any m failures. Used in: CDs, QR codes, RAID 6, cloud storage (S3, Azure). Well-understood, efficient.

questions.question: What is the tradeoff of erasure coding vs replication?

options.text: Erasure coding: less storage, but higher CPU for encode/decode and higher latency for reads

questions.explanation: Erasure coding tradeoffs: storage efficient, but: CPU overhead for encoding/decoding, read latency (may need multiple fragments), repair bandwidth (reconstruct from k fragments). Best for cold/archival data.

questions.question: What does RS(10,4) mean in erasure coding?

options.text: 10 data chunks + 4 parity chunks; can recover from any 4 chunk failures

questions.explanation: RS(10,4): Reed-Solomon with k=10 data, m=4 parity. Total 14 chunks. Any 10 chunks can reconstruct data. Storage overhead: 4/10 = 40%. Survives 4 simultaneous failures.

questions.question: Which storage systems use erasure coding?
questions.explanation: Erasure coding widely used: S3 (11 9s durability), Azure, Google Cloud Storage, HDFS 3.0+, Ceph, MinIO. Cloud providers use it for cost-effective durability at scale.

questions.question: When is replication preferred over erasure coding?

options.text: For hot data with frequent reads where low latency is critical

questions.explanation: Prefer replication for: hot data (fast reads from any replica), low latency requirements, small files (erasure coding overhead not worth it). Erasure coding better for: cold data, large files, archival.

questions.question: What is the repair bandwidth problem in erasure coding?

options.text: Recovering one failed chunk requires reading k chunks, consuming significant network bandwidth

questions.explanation: Repair bandwidth: to recover 1 lost chunk in RS(10,4), must read 10 chunks. If chunk is 1GB, repair needs 10GB network transfer. At scale, this is significant. Local reconstruction codes help.

questions.question: What are Local Reconstruction Codes (LRC)?

options.text: Erasure codes with local parity groups that reduce repair bandwidth by enabling local recovery

questions.explanation: LRC: add local parity within groups. Example: Azure LRC(12,2,2)—12 data, 2 local parity, 2 global parity. Single failure: recover from local group (fewer reads). Reduces repair bandwidth significantly.

questions.question: How does HDFS use erasure coding?

options.text: HDFS 3.0+ supports erasure coding as alternative to replication, configurable per directory

questions.explanation: HDFS 3.0+: erasure coding support. Configure per directory: cold data uses EC, hot data uses replication. Reduces storage by ~50% for cold data. Policies: RS(6,3), RS(10,4), etc.

questions.question: What is the storage overhead formula for erasure coding?
questions.explanation: Storage overhead = m/k. RS(10,4): 4/10 = 40% overhead. RS(6,3): 3/6 = 50% overhead. Compare to 3x replication: 200% overhead. Choose k,m based on durability needs and storage budget.

questions.question: A cloud provider wants to store 1EB of archival data with 99.999999999% durability. Best approach?

options.text: Erasure coding (e.g., RS(10,4)) across multiple availability zones

questions.explanation: 1EB archival: erasure coding is ideal. RS(10,4) across AZs: 40% overhead (vs 200% for 3x replication), survives 4 failures, 11 9s durability achievable. Cost-effective at scale. This is how S3 works.
